scenes.name: Frankie Goes to Hollywood
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Veteranos de la escena glam punk del Eric's (Holly Johnson de Big in Japan, Paul Rutherford de los Spitfire Boys) más «the lads», con imagen sadomasoquista y homosexualidad declarada: los «Disco Pistols». Atrapados en un contrato humillante con ZTT, Horn graba «Relax» (1983) casi sin ellos, a ritmo de Hi-NRG con Fairlight y Linn sincronizados; la prohibición de la BBC la lleva al número uno. Morley planea una trilogía sobre sexo, guerra y religión: «Two Tribes» (nueve semanas en el número uno, con camisetas «FRANKIE SAY»), «The Power of Love». Welcome to the Pleasuredome decepciona, Estados Unidos los ve como unos Village People y acaban sin fans de verdad: anuncio del regreso de las boy bands. «¿No tuvieron alguna vez la sensación de que los engañaron?»

podcast.title: David Bowie Fan
podcast.body: Johnson was a huge fan of David Bowie, an influence that likely played a role in his own theatrical stage presence and embrace of provocative imagery. "He was also a huge David Bowie fan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock

podcast.title: Impact of Bowie's "Coming Out"
podcast.body: Holly Johnson of Frankie Goes to Hollywood credited David Bowie's "coming out" statement in January 1972 as having changed his life. Bowie's public bravery gave Johnson the courage to be who he was. "Boy George of Culture Club and Holly Johnson of Frankie Ghost of Hollywood say that their lives were changed by Bowie's comments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Out Gay Frontman
podcast.body: Holly Johnson, the frontman for Frankie Goes to Hollywood, was an openly gay man. His real name was William, but he adopted the name Holly in high school, inspired by the transvestite Holly Woodlawn, who was famously mentioned in Lou Reed's song "Walk on the Wild Side." "Holly Johnson, an out-game man whose real name was William."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Early Days of LGBTQ Rock

xref.title: Origins at Eric's Club (1980)
xref.body: The band's beginnings trace back to 1980 in Liverpool, where most of the members were regulars at a club called Eric's. This venue served as a formative hub for the group before their rise to fame. "The beginnings of the band go back to 1980 and the frontman was Holly Johnson."

xref.title: Breakup and Internal Strife (1987)
xref.body: The band officially broke up in 1987 after the release of their second album, "Liverpool," due to waning public interest and severe internal conflicts, including a backstage fistfight between singer Holly Johnson and bass player Mark O'Toole at a Wembley show in January. "The band broke up in 1987 following the release of their second album called Liverpool. They had basically worn out their welcome with the public, and things weren't going well internally."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: VH1's "Bands Reunited" (2003)
xref.body: In 2003, all members were asked to appear on the VH1 show "Bands Reunited." Holly Johnson participated only through an interview, refusing to perform or engage in any subsequent revival efforts. "Everyone was asked to appear on that VH1 show called Bands Reunited. Holly did not want any part of the TV show or any subsequent revival, but he did appear on the show just the same, just an interview, though, no performance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Holly Johnson's Failed Trademark Attempt (2007)
xref.body: To prevent other members from using the band's name without him, Holly Johnson attempted to register "Frankie Goes to Hollywood" as his personal trademark, but a judge ruled against him on June 7, 2007, deeming his attempt frivolous and ordering him to pay approximately 3,200 pounds in court costs. "Holly tried to register the name, Frankie goes to Hollywood as a trademark owned by him, thereby denying everything else to things like the name for gigs and t-shirts and CDs and DVDs, everything."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 3

xref.title: Reunion with New Singer Ryan Maloy (2007)
xref.body: The judge's ruling against Holly Johnson's trademark attempt opened the door for a Frankie Goes to Hollywood revival, which featured a new singer named Ryan Maloy. "That opened the door to the Frankie Revival, featuring a new singer named Ryan Maloy, and Holly had to pay about 3,200 pounds in court costs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Attempt to Replace Singer Holly Johnson
xref.body: Following internal strife, Liverpool singer Pete Wylie was secretly approached and asked if he would like to replace Holly Johnson as the band's new singer, but Wylie declined the offer. "Then a Liverpool singer named Pete Wiley was secretly called. The call went something like this. Hey, you know what? We're sick of Holly. Would you like to be our new singer? But Pete said, no, I don't want anything to do with this."

xref.title: Impact of Bowie's "Coming Out"
xref.body: Boy George of Culture Club openly stated that his life was profoundly changed by David Bowie's public comments in January 1972 about being gay. Bowie's statement gave him the courage to embrace and be true to his own identity. "Boy George of Culture Club and Holly Johnson of Frankie Ghost of Hollywood say that their lives were changed by Bowie's comments."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Inspiration for LGBTQ+ Individuals
xref.body: Bowie's public comments about his sexuality in 1972 struck a chord with thousands who were afraid to come out, giving them courage and a sense of shared identity with a famous figure. Figures like Boy George of Culture Club and Holly Johnson of Frankie Goes to Hollywood have stated that Bowie's comments changed their lives. "Bowie gave them the courage to be who they were."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: New Name for Frankie Goes to Hollywood
xref.body: This name was adopted by the former members of Frankie Goes to Hollywood to avoid further legal issues after Holly Johnson's failed attempt to trademark the original band name. "Well, working under the name for Bidden Holly Wood to avoid further legal issues."
